{{Short description|About maxima and minima of functions}} 
{{redirect|Fermat's theorem (stationary points)|other theorems named after Pierre de Fermat|Fermat's theorem}}
[[File:Interior extremum graph.svg|thumb|A differentiable function graph with lines tangent to the minimum and maximum. The interior extremum theorem guarantees that these lines will always be horizontal.]]
In [[calculus]] and [[real analysis]], the '''interior extremum theorem''' states that any [[maximum and minimum|local extremum]] of a real function at which it is [[differentiable function|differentiable]] is a [[stationary point]]. It is also known as '''Fermat's theorem''', named after the French mathematician [[Pierre de Fermat]].

The interior extremum theorem gives a [[necessity and sufficiency#Necessity|necessary]], but not [[necessity and sufficiency#Sufficiency|sufficient]] condition for local extrema at which the function is differentiable, as some stationary points are not local extrema.

The [[second derivative]], if non-zero, can be used to determine whether a local extremum at which the function is twice differentiable is a maximum or a minimum. However, the second derivative can be zero at local extrema.

== History ==
[[Pierre de Fermat]] proposed in a collection of treatises titled ''Maxima et minima'' a method to find maximum or minimum, similar to the modern interior extremum theorem using an approach he called [[adequality]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Fikhtengol'ts |first=G.M. |title=The Fundamentals of Mathematical Analysis |publisher=[[Pergamon Press]] |year=1965 |isbn=978-0-08-013473-4 |doi=10.1016/C2013-0-02242-6}}</ref>{{Rp|page=|pages=456–457}}<ref name=":0" />{{Rp|page=2}}<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Breger |first=Herbert |date=2013 |title=Fermat's Analysis of Extreme Values and Tangents |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/43695566 |journal=Studia Leibnitiana |volume=45 |issue=1 |pages=20–41 |issn=0039-3185}}</ref> After [[Marin Mersenne]] passed the treatises onto [[René Descartes]], Descartes was doubtful, remarking "if [...] he speaks of wanting to send you still more papers, I beg of you to ask him to think them out more carefully than those preceding".<ref name=":0" />{{Rp|page=3}} Descartes later agreed that the method was valid.<ref name=":0" />{{Rp|page=8}}

==Statement==
One way to state the interior extremum theorem is that, if a function has a local [[Maxima and minima|extremum]] at some point and is [[differentiable function|differentiable]] there, then the function's derivative at that point must be zero. In precise mathematical language:

:Let <math>f\colon (a,b) \rightarrow \mathbb{R}</math> be a function from an [[open interval]] {{tmath|(a,b)}} to {{tmath|\R}}, and suppose that <math>x_0 \in (a,b)</math> is a point where <math>f</math> has a local extremum. If <math>f</math> is differentiable at <math>x_0</math>, then <math>f'(x_0) = 0</math>.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Bronshtein |first1=I. N. |last2=Semendyayev |first2=K. A. |date=1972 |title=A Guide Book to Mathematics |publisher=Springer |doi=10.1007/978-1-4684-6288-3|isbn=978-1-4684-6290-6 }}</ref>{{Rp|page=377}}

Another way to understand the theorem is via the [[contrapositive]] statement: if the derivative of a function at any point is not zero, then there is not a local extremum at that point. Formally:
:If <math>f</math> is differentiable at <math>x_0 \in (a,b)</math>, and <math>f'(x_0) \neq 0</math>, then <math>x_0</math> is not a local extremum of <math>f</math>.

===Corollary===
Every global extremum of a function ''f'' on a [[Domain of a function|domain]] ''A'' occurs only at the [[boundary (topology)|boundary]] of ''A'', non-differentiable points, or stationary points.
If <math>x_0</math> is a global extremum of ''f'', then one of the following is true:<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last=Monks |first=Kenneth M |date=February 20, 2023 |title=Fermat's Method for Finding Maxima and Minima |url=https://old.maa.org/sites/default/files/images/upload_library/46/Barnett_TRIUMPHS_MiniPSPs/MiniPSP_FermatsMethod_2023_02_20.pdf |journal=[[MAA Convergence]]}}</ref>{{Rp|page=1}}
* '''boundary:''' <math>x_0</math> is in the boundary of ''A''
* '''non-differentiable:''' ''f'' is not differentiable at <math>x_0</math>
* '''stationary point:''' <math>f'(x_0)=0</math>

The function {{tmath|1=f(x)=x^3}} has no extrema. The function  {{tmath|1=f(x)=x^3-x}} has no global extrema, although it has local extrema.

===Extension===

A similar statement holds for the [[partial derivatives]] of [[Multivariate function|multivariate functions]]. Suppose that some real-valued function of the real numbers <math>f = f(t_1, t_2, \ldots,t_k)</math> has an extremum at a point <math>C</math>, defined by <math>C = (a_1, a_2,\ldots ,a_k)</math>. If <math>f</math> is differentiable at <math>C</math>, then:<math display="block">\frac{\partial}{\partial t_i}f(C)=0</math>for each <math>i = 1, 2, \ldots ,k</math>.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Bhattacharya |first=Bhargab B. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=YejsjRjHiJ0C&dq=multivariable+fermat's+theorem&pg=PA16 |title=Algorithms, Architectures and Information Systems Security |date=2009 |publisher=[[World Scientific]] |isbn=978-981-283-624-3 |language=en}}</ref>{{Rp|page=16}}

The statement can also be extended to [[differentiable manifolds]]. If <math>f : M \to \mathbb{R}</math> is a [[Differentiable manifold#Differentiable functions|differentiable function]] on a manifold <math>M</math>, then its local extrema must be [[Critical point (mathematics)|critical points]] of <math>f</math>, in particular points where the [[exterior derivative]] <math>df</math> is zero.<ref>{{cite web|title=Is Fermat's theorem about local extrema true for smooth manifolds? |date=August 11, 2015 |url=https://math.stackexchange.com/q/1392981 |work=[[Stack Exchange]] |accessdate=21 April 2017}}</ref>{{better source|date=January 2023}}

==Applications==
The interior extremum theorem is central for determining [[maxima and minima]] of [[piecewise function|piecewise differentiable functions]] of one variable: an extremum is either a [[stationary point]] (that is, a [[Zero of a function|zero]] of the derivative), a non-differentiable point (that is a point where the function is not [[differentiable function|differentiable]]), or a [[boundary point]] of the [[domain of a function|domain of the function]]. Since the number of these points is typically finite, the computation of the values of the function at these points provides the maximum and the minimum, simply by comparing the obtained values.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Brinkhuis |first1=Jan |last2=Tikhomirov |first2=Vladimir |url=https://archive.org/details/optimizationinsi0000brin/page/24/mode/2up?q=%22fermat+theorem%22&view=theater |title=Optimization: Insights and Applications |year=2005 |publisher=Princeton University Press |isbn=978-0-691-10287-0 |url-access=limited }}</ref>{{Rp|page=25}}<ref name=":0" />{{Rp|page=1}}

==Proof==
Suppose that <math>x_0</math> is a local maximum.  (A similar argument applies if <math>x_0</math> is a local minimum.) Then there is some [[Neighbourhood (mathematics)|neighbourhood]] around <math>x_0</math> such that <math>f(x_0) \ge f(x)</math> for all <math>x</math> within that neighborhood. If <math>x > x_0</math>, then the [[difference quotient]] <math>\frac{f(x) - f(x_0)}{x - x_0}</math> is non-positive for <math>x</math> in this neighborhood. This implies
<math display="block">
\lim_{x\rightarrow x_0^+}\frac{f(x) - f(x_0)}{x - x_0} \le 0.
</math>
Similarly, if <math>x < x_0</math>, then the difference quotient is non-negative, and so
<math display="block">
\lim_{x\rightarrow x_0^-}\frac{f(x) - f(x_0)}{x - x_0} \geq 0.
</math>
Since <math>f</math> is differentiable, the above limits must both be equal to <math>f'(x_0)</math>. This is only possible if both limits are equal to 0, so <math>f'(x_0) = 0</math>.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Canuto |first1=Claudio |title=Mathematical Analysis I |last2=Tabacco |first2=Anita |publisher=Springer |year=2015 |isbn=978-3-319-12771-2 |edition=2nd |doi=10.1007/978-3-319-12772-9}}</ref>{{Rp|page=182}}
